beats: Hook: describing 300 qubits takes about 2 x 10^90 complex numbers (2^300), more than the atoms in the observable universe (about 10^80, an estimate); 300 separate qubits take 600. Everything in between is entanglement. (line_qc_tensor_ledger_tower: a short row of cards on the desk, a tower of ledgers into the stars.) Cast as in QC04-01: the tinkerer and the friend.

Two qubits: the basis is every pairing of the single-qubit bases, |00>, |01>, |10>, |11> (tensor product, 40:55-46:42), like two drinks times two snacks making four trays (line_qc_tensor_combo_menu); a two-qubit state is four amplitudes, outcome probabilities |alpha_ij|^2.

Measure only qubit A (48:09-49:27): add the matching outcomes, P(A=0) = |alpha00|^2 + |alpha01|^2 (line_qc_tensor_combo_menu again: ask only about the drink and add the two trays with the cup). Skip the student dialogue 49:27-52:38.
Each added qubit doubles the basis: 2^n (52:09-54:27); reuse line_two_lanterns (every fork doubles the paths) and line_heap for the pile of amplitudes.

The tensor product of two single-qubit states: each of the four amplitudes is (amplitude of A) x (amplitude of B), like a loom where every crossing is set by its warp thread and its weft thread (line_qc_tensor_loom); her example (|00>+|10>)/sqrt2 = |+>|0> (54:27-58:56, clip 54:35-55:01).

Product vs. entangled: a product state has one description per qubit, like two solo dancers; an entangled state can only be described as a pair, like a lift where each dancer leans on the other (line_qc_tensor_solo_duet). The Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, the EPR pair (63:04-64:45): two linked rings carved from one block, no seam to split them along (line_qc_tensor_carved_rings). Skip the student dialogue 63:36-64:29.

"Most states are entangled" (59:06-60:57; clips 59:06-59:37 and 60:57-61:23, "a much larger space than the tensor product"): four free amplitudes vs. the constrained product family (line_qc_tensor_ring_crate: a crate of linked carvings beside a tiny tray of separable pairs). Honest wording: almost every state, picked at random, is entangled; that alone is not a speed-up.

Her 2024 exercise (Q24-03 notes p5-p6): write a program that tests product vs. entangled; for two qubits it is one comparison, alpha00 x alpha11 = alpha01 x alpha10 (line_qc_tensor_corner_check; reuse line_balance); the Bell state fails it (1/2 vs. 0).
Takeaway: an n-qubit state is 2^n amplitudes (69:30-71:21); a product state needs about 2n. Next: what an entangled pair can and cannot do (QC04-04).

Cover (line_qc_cover_04_03; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the tinkerer and the friend each pull on one ring of a big carving of two linked rings carved from one block and cannot part them; a two-piece puzzle lies easily separated at their feet.
